proof: Emulators recreate a console so they can run its library. Retro Porting Toolkit takes a different route: it recompiles one game at a time, preserving the original game logic while replacing the hardware constraints around it. That trades broad compatibility for deeper control over rendering, input, networking, and behavior, and it builds directly on decades of knowledge from the emulation community.

Correctness is measured, not asserted. Builds are checked against the reference cores the community already trusts, melonDS on the Nintendo DS and the Beetle VB core on the Virtual Boy, and against the attract demo sitting in the game's own ROM: prerecorded input that plays the same way every time, so the comparison does not wait on someone playing. Measuring is also what makes an honest answer possible when the answer is unflattering. PlayStation has seven core-team games you can play. The Virtual Boy has exactly one, and vbrecomp still calls itself a tech demo. Every project page says how far it goes.
philosophy: Go native. Windows, Linux, macOS, Android, even the browser. No emulator core in sight.
See more of the world. Adaptive widescreen up to 21:9 in games like Tomba! 2 and Mega Man Zero.
Break the old limits. 60 FPS patches, CD-quality MSU-1 soundtracks, voxel 3D remixes, and mod loaders that never touch your original ROM.
Swap the hardware. Spin WarioWare: Twisted! with your phone or a DualSense, and let real local weather drive Boktai's solar sensor.
Change the words. Runtime text replacement powers Tsumu Light's English fan translation and NES text overrides.
Play together. Shared netplay, rollback, save states, and rewind (recomp-net and retcomm-rbengine) that every ecosystem can pick up.
constraintsIntro: Across the mod systems one rule holds: features layer over your own copy of the game while it runs, rather than patching it. Most projects verify your dump's fingerprint before anything starts, and the additions are opt-in switches rather than a second version of the game. Turn widescreen off and the original 4:3 output comes back byte for byte. That is what makes everything below safe to try.

stories.title: The map was already loaded. The screen was hiding it.
stories.body: Game Boy Advance games often load much of their map and overworld into memory at once, and the size of the screen was the only thing keeping it out of sight. Mega Man Zero opens the logical view past the original 240 pixels, 288 recommended and the wider settings still validation targets, so a threat is on screen before it is on top of you. Enemies keep their original spawn rules, so things can still appear near the new edges.
stories.alt: Mega Man Zero running with the view opened past the original Game Boy Advance width

stories.title: Boktai still runs on sunlight. Yours.
stories.body: The cartridge carried a real light sensor: the solar gun charged from actual sunlight, and the undead could only be sealed while you had light. A community build keeps the requirement and moves the sensor. Give it a postal code and the weather where you are drives the gauge, empty at night, a bar or three under heavy cloud, full in clear midday, with the full sun point adjustable. Give it no postal code and nothing ever leaves your machine.
stories.alt: Boktai running with its solar gauge driven by local weather

stories.title: The words can change while the game runs.
stories.body: Faxanadu is the showcase for the NES framework's text override: dialogue and glyphs are replaced at runtime from a data file, with hot reload, so an edit shows up in the running game about a second later. The same idea carries a whole game on PlayStation, where Tsumu Light, a puzzle game that never left Japan, now reads in English without the disc being touched.
stories.alt: Faxanadu running as a native PC application

platformNote.title: Each console teaches the next.
platformNote.body: The DS recompiler's second processor started as the Game Boy Advance one, because both are ARM. The CD-i's 68000 front end came out of the Genesis work. On the Super Nintendo, the Cx4, Super FX, DSP-1, and SA-1 cartridge chips are modeled once in the shared runtime, each brought up against the game that needed it, so the next game that needs one already has it.

action.videoTitle: Street Fighter Alpha 3 Recomp is out now
action.alt: Street Fighter Alpha 3 running as a native build
action.blurb: Roughly five minutes of game-specific work took this from disc to a running native build, done outside the core team. There is no public download. The video is the record.

action.videoTitle: Character replacement running in Super Mario World
action.alt: Super Mario World running with a replacement character
action.blurb: Not a sprite swap: movement, abilities, animation, and sound all change. A disassembly names 1,937 of the game's 2,074 functions, which is why a hook can land on the routine that moves Mario.

action.videoTitle: Metroid Prime Hunters Recomp is out now
action.alt: Metroid Prime Hunters running with mouse aiming
action.blurb: WASD and mouse aiming stand in for the stylus scheme, in a public alpha. The DS framework underneath is still research. The game runs ahead of it.

action.videoTitle: Save states and rewind, shown off in Tomba!
action.alt: Tomba! with the rewind timeline open
action.blurb: Tomba! is what you watch. The rollback engine is the point: it was lifted out of the PlayStation runtime with the platform-specific types removed, so any host can pick it up.

featuredPost.title: Building & Enhancing Recomps: Ecosystem Updates
featuredPost.blurb: Where every ecosystem stands, including the parts that are barely standing: the GameCube's own system menu running in full, calendar and memory card manager included, the CD-i's player software loading a disc as far as Hotel Mario's title card, and one green dot from the Original Xbox research that traveled a real boot ROM, a retail kernel, and a GPU command stream to get there.
